analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to cover cheaper generics and biosimilars at lower cost with fewer access hurdles.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with bipartisan sponsorship from three House members, the bill was referred to two committees and has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill requires Medicare Part D prescription drug plans to put any cheaper generic version of a brand-name drug, and at least two cheaper biosimilar versions of a brand-name biologic, on their list of covered drugs in a preferred tier with lower out-of-pocket costs for patients. It also bars plans from making those cheaper drugs harder to get than the expensive original — no extra prior-authorization requirements, step therapy, or other hurdles that push patients toward the pricier product. It applies to plan years starting in 2027 or later.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in standalone Part D drug plans. When a generic or biosimilar costs less than the brand-name original, they would be guaranteed access to the cheaper version on a lower-cost tier, and plans could not steer them back to the expensive original through prior authorization or step therapy.

how_it_helps.text: Plans must place each covered generic that costs less than its brand-name reference drug in a preferred position — a more favorable tier with lower patient out-of-pocket costs [S2].
Plans must include at least two covered biosimilars priced below the reference biological product in a preferred position [S2].
Plans may not impose prior authorization, step therapy, or other access limits on the required generics and biosimilars that are more restrictive than what applies to the pricier reference drug [S2].
The requirements take effect for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would lose sales when cheaper generics and biosimilars must be given preferred placement. Part D plan sponsors would lose some control over their formularies and utilization-management tools, which could put upward pressure on premiums or plan design.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The standard is tied to wholesale acquisition cost, a list price that often does not reflect the actual net price after rebates and discounts, so in some cases the 'cheaper' drug on paper may not be cheaper in practice [S2].
The bill applies only to standalone Part D prescription drug plan (PDP) sponsors; Medicare Advantage plans that include drug coverage are not covered by this requirement [S2].
Requiring preferred placement and limiting utilization management removes tools insurers use to control costs, which could put upward pressure on Part D premiums for all enrollees.
Requiring two biosimilars only bites in markets where two cheaper biosimilars exist, so for many brand-name biologics the provision changes nothing until competitors launch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing high drug costs, guaranteed access to a cheaper generic or biosimilar on a lower tier is a direct, tangible benefit. The costs — less formulary flexibility for insurers and possible premium pressure — are real but modest, and the bill's reach is limited by its PDP-only scope and its reliance on list prices that may overstate the discount patients actually see.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late March 2026 and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, where it sits with no hearings, markup, or vote scheduled; Congress is still in session, so it is not yet dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Doris Matsui introduced the bill on March 27, 2026, joined by Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R) and Jake Auchincloss (D) [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S4].
The bill has two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat, and no further action since referral [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no vote or committee action yet, no one has won or lost; brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers benefit from the delay because their formulary control and pricing remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; insurers and drug makers keep status quo

for.name: Rep. Doris Matsui
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require Part D plans to cover cheaper generics and biosimilars in preferred positions [S1][S2].

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican cosponsor joined the Democratic sponsor — but no one has publicly opposed the bill and no vote has occurred; it simply sits in two committees with only two cosponsors.

industries.note: Whenever a generic or biosimilar undercuts the brand-name price, plans must give the cheaper copy a preferred tier with lower patient costs, cutting into brand-name sales. Patients get the cheaper option instead of being steered to the expensive original.

The bill guarantees their cheaper products a preferred formulary position in Part D and bars plans from restricting access relative to the reference drug, increasing their volume and giving their gains to patients in lower out-of-pocket costs.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D prescription drug plan sponsors (insurers)
industries.note: Plans lose discretion over formulary tiers and cannot use prior authorization or step therapy to steer patients to the pricier reference drug, which limits their cost-management tools and could pressure premiums. Their interest in keeping those tools runs against patient access to cheaper drugs.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is at the very start of the process with only two cosponsors and dual committee referral. Most bills at this stage — especially those touching drug pricing and insurance design, where Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce both have jurisdiction — never receive a hearing or markup. Unless the sponsor builds substantially more support or the provisions attach to a larger Medicare package, it will likely remain in committee for the rest of the 119th Congress.
